title: Six Drops on the Rope
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
wiifm: This week has been about how minds work alone. The Prince is about how they work in a room full of rivals: how power is gained, held and lost when people are not as good as they say they are. Its author is the most misunderstood writer in politics, a loyal civil servant who was tortured, sacked and exiled before he wrote a word of it. You will follow Niccolò Machiavelli through Renaissance Florence and the camp of a ruthless young warlord, and leave with a clear-eyed, usable view of authority, reputation and timing in any organisation, including your own.

ch.h: A boy and a borrowed Livy
b: Niccolò Machiavelli was born in Florence on the third of May 1469, the same year that Lorenzo de' Medici, later called the Magnificent, became the city's unofficial ruler. The Machiavellis were an old Florentine family with little money left. His father Bernardo was a lawyer who loved books he could not afford.

Bernardo kept a diary, which survives, and it records a bargain that shaped his son's life. In 1475 a printer agreed to give him a copy of Livy's history of Rome in return for compiling an index of its place names. Years later Bernardo paid to have the volume bound, and his teenage son took it to the binder. Niccolò grew up on Livy, on the long story of a republic that rose by its own arms and its citizens' virtue.

Florence in those years was officially a republic but was run, behind the scenes, by the Medici banking family. It was a city of painters, bankers, factions and conspiracies. In 1478, when Niccolò was nine, the rival Pazzi family stabbed Lorenzo's brother Giuliano to death during Mass in the cathedral. The conspirators were hanged from the windows of the government palace. A boy in Florence learned early that politics could be lethal.

Machiavelli did not go to university. He was taught Latin and arithmetic by private tutors, and he read the Roman historians and poets with the hunger of someone who could not take books for granted. It gave him a lifelong habit that runs through The Prince: whenever he wants to make a point about his own time, he reaches for an ancient example, and treats Roman generals and Florentine bankers as if they were sitting at the same table.
ch.cap: Young Niccolo carries the bound Livy through Florence

ch.h: The prophet who had no army
b: In 1494 the King of France, Charles the Eighth, marched into Italy with a huge army and modern artillery. Italian states that had played elegant diplomatic games for decades collapsed in weeks. The Medici were driven out of Florence. Into the gap stepped a Dominican friar, Girolamo Savonarola, whose sermons against luxury and corruption held the city spellbound. Florentines burned their mirrors, paintings and fine clothes in great bonfires of the vanities.

Machiavelli, then in his twenties, heard Savonarola preach and was not converted. He was impressed by the friar's power over a crowd and unimpressed by everything else. Savonarola fell foul of the Pope, lost the people's support, and in May 1498 was hanged and burned in the main square of Florence.

Machiavelli drew a lesson he would put plainly in The Prince. All armed prophets have conquered, he wrote, and unarmed ones have come to ruin. Moses could compel belief when it faltered. Savonarola could not. Persuasion is wonderful, but people's moods change, and a leader needs some means of holding them when belief wears thin.
ch.cap: Savonarola preaches as the bonfire of the vanities burns

b: Within weeks of Savonarola's death, in June 1498, the twenty-nine-year-old Machiavelli was appointed head of the Second Chancery of the Florentine republic, and soon also secretary to the Ten of War, the committee that ran diplomacy and defence. He had no famous name and no fortune. He got the job through ability and connections, and for fourteen years he was one of the busiest public servants in Italy.

He was sent on missions to the King of France, to the Holy Roman Emperor, to the Pope and to a string of Italian rulers. Florence was rich but militarily weak, and his job was to buy time with words. He wrote quick, vivid reports back home, watching how powerful men actually behaved rather than how they claimed to.

From these years came his most practical conviction. Florence relied on hired mercenary soldiers, and he watched them fail. In the long war to recapture the rebel city of Pisa, they were slow, expensive and unreliable, because men paid to fight have little reason to die. In 1506 he persuaded the republic to raise a citizen militia, and in 1509 that militia helped force Pisa's surrender. In The Prince he would insist that a ruler who depends on other people's arms stands on borrowed ground.

His French missions taught him a humbling lesson about reputation. At the court of Louis the Twelfth the French dismissed Florence as a city that paid late and fought badly. Machiavelli noted that the French respected only those who were armed or who could pay, and that clever arguments counted for very little without one or the other. A state without its own strength, he concluded, is treated as nothing, however eloquent its ambassadors.
ch.cap: Machiavelli's citizen militia marches on Pisa

ch.h: The duke in the square at Cesena
b: The ruler who fascinated him most was Cesare Borgia, son of Pope Alexander the Sixth. Using his father's money and French troops, Cesare carved out a state for himself in the Romagna, in central Italy. In 1502 Machiavelli spent months as Florence's envoy at his court, and he watched closely.

The Romagna had been lawless, so Cesare appointed a hard, efficient lieutenant, Remirro de Orco, who restored order with great cruelty. When the job was done and the cruelty had made Remirro hated, Cesare had him killed. One morning in December 1502 the people of Cesena found his body lying in two pieces in the square, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside it. The ferocity of the spectacle, Machiavelli wrote, left the people at once satisfied and stunned.

Weeks later, at Senigallia on the last day of 1502, Cesare invited a group of mercenary captains who had plotted against him to a reconciliation, then had them seized. Two were strangled that night, and two more in the following weeks. Machiavelli was nearby and reported the events to Florence.

In The Prince Cesare becomes his model of a new ruler who did nearly everything right and still failed. When Alexander the Sixth died suddenly in 1503, Cesare was himself gravely ill, his support melted away and he lost almost everything. Machiavelli blamed one mistake: allowing an old enemy to become Pope Julius the Second. Never trust, he concluded, that new favours make great men forget old injuries.
ch.cap: Cesena wakes to find Remirro's body in the square

b: In 1512 the Spanish army, allied with the Pope, attacked Florence's territory and sacked the nearby town of Prato. Machiavelli's militia broke and ran. The republic collapsed, its leader Piero Soderini fled, and the Medici came back. In November Machiavelli was dismissed from all his posts and barred from the government palace.

Worse followed. In February 1513 a plot against the Medici was discovered, and a list of names was found on one of the conspirators. Machiavelli's was on it. There is no evidence he was involved, but he was arrested and tortured with the strappado, in which the prisoner's hands are tied behind his back and he is hoisted by a rope and dropped. In a rueful sonnet written from his cell to Giuliano de' Medici, he mentioned shackles on his legs and six drops of the rope on his shoulders. He confessed nothing, and later told a friend he had borne it with a courage that surprised even himself.

Then fortune turned. In March 1513 Giovanni de' Medici was elected Pope Leo the Tenth, the first Florentine Pope, and the city celebrated with an amnesty. Machiavelli walked out of prison, unemployed, disgraced and forty-three years old, with a wife and young children to support.
ch.cap: Under the strappado rope, Machiavelli writes his sonnet

b: He retreated to his family's small farm at Sant'Andrea in Percussina, a few miles south of Florence. On the tenth of December 1513 he wrote one of the most famous letters in Italian literature to his friend Francesco Vettori, Florence's ambassador in Rome.

By day, he wrote, he snared thrushes, argued with woodcutters and played cards and backgammon with the innkeeper, the butcher and the miller, shouting over small stakes. In the evening he came home, took off his muddy clothes at the door and put on the robes of a court official. Dressed properly, he entered the ancient courts of great men, asked them the reasons for their actions, and they answered him. For four hours, he said, he felt no boredom, forgot every trouble and did not fear poverty or death.

From those conversations, he told Vettori, he had composed a little work on principalities: what they are, what kinds there are, how they are gained, how they are kept and why they are lost. That little work was The Prince. He hoped it would show the Medici that his fifteen years in statecraft had not been spent asleep, and win him a job. He eventually dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici, the Pope's nephew. It brought him nothing.

The book is short, twenty-six chapters, written in plain, brisk Italian rather than the scholarly Latin that serious political writing was expected to use. It moves from types of state, to armies, to the qualities of a ruler, and ends with a burning appeal. Italy, he wrote, was more enslaved than the Hebrews and more scattered than the Athenians, without a head, without order, beaten, despoiled and overrun. He called on the Medici to be the house that would set it free.
ch.cap: In court robes, Machiavelli questions the ancients by candlelight

b: What made the book shocking was its starting point. Many writers, Machiavelli said, have imagined republics and principalities that have never existed. He wanted instead to follow the effective truth of things. A ruler who tries to be good in every respect among so many who are not good will come to ruin. So a prince must learn how not to be good, and use that knowledge or not according to necessity.

The famous question follows. Is it better to be loved or feared? Ideally both, he says, but since that is hard, it is safer to be feared, because love is held by a chain of obligation that people break whenever it suits them, while fear is held by a dread of punishment that never fails. But he immediately adds the vital condition: a prince must be feared without being hated. And the surest way to avoid hatred is to leave people's property and their women alone. Men, he wrote, forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of their inheritance.

Cruelty, he argued, can be well used or badly used. Well used means all at once, out of necessity, and then turned as far as possible to the benefit of the people. Injuries should be done all together, so they are tasted less and offend less. Benefits should be given little by little, so they are savoured more.

He also wrote that a ruler must be both a fox, to recognise traps, and a lion, to frighten wolves. And because people judge more by the eye than by the hand, a ruler need not have every virtue, but must seem to. Few people touch what you are. Everyone sees what you appear to be.

Notice how practical this is. Machiavelli is not telling rulers to be cruel for pleasure. He is telling them that reputation is a resource, that it is built from what people see, and that kindness handed out in the wrong way can cause more suffering than firmness. He pointed to the Florentines who, to avoid seeming cruel, let the city of Pistoia tear itself apart in faction fighting.
ch.cap: A masked prince sits between the fox and the lion

b: The deepest idea in the book is the struggle between virtù and fortuna. Virtù is not virtue in the moral sense. It means ability, energy, boldness, the capacity to act decisively. Fortuna is chance, the circumstances no one controls.

Machiavelli thought fortune governed perhaps half of our actions and left the other half to us. He compared it to a violent river that floods the plains, tears up trees and carries away buildings. Nobody can stop the flood once it comes. But in calm weather people can build dykes and embankments, so that when the river rises it is channelled or its force is weaker. Ruin comes to those who did nothing while the sun was shining.

He also noticed that the same behaviour succeeds in one season and fails in another. A cautious man prospers in cautious times and is ruined when times demand boldness, because people rarely change their nature. His own militia had been his embankment. When the flood came at Prato, it had not been high enough.

Fortune, in his most notorious image, is like a woman who favours the young and the bold, and who must be mastered rather than courted. It is a line that has rightly made modern readers wince, and it reflects the attitudes of his time. The point he was reaching for is that in moments of crisis, it is usually better to be impetuous than cautious, because waiting rarely improves a deteriorating position.
ch.cap: The river floods; the embankment holds it back

ch.h: The book that outlived its author
b: The Medici never really took him back. He wrote his longer and more republican Discourses on Livy, which argues that free republics, with their quarrels and many voices, are more durable than princes. He wrote a comedy, The Mandrake, which was a hit, and in 1520 the Medici commissioned him to write a history of Florence. In 1527 the Medici were expelled again and the restored republic saw him as their man. Passed over once more, he died in Florence on the twenty-first of June 1527.

The Prince was printed only in 1532, five years after his death. In 1559 the Catholic Church placed his works on its Index of Prohibited Books, and in English his first name became a byword for the devil. Shakespeare could refer to the murderous Machiavel and expect his audience to understand.

Readers have argued ever since about what he meant. Some, like the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, thought The Prince was a satire, a warning to the people disguised as advice to rulers. Most modern scholars think it was sincere, but narrower than its reputation: a handbook for a new ruler in a broken, invaded Italy, ending in a passionate plea to liberate the country from foreign armies. Isaiah Berlin argued that Machiavelli's real shock was showing that political ends and Christian morality could conflict, with no guarantee of a painless answer.

For a modern reader the value is not permission to be ruthless. It is the discipline of seeing the effective truth of things: how people actually behave, what actually holds an organisation together, and how to build your embankments before the flood.
ch.cap: The Prince comes off the press, five years after him

take: Deal with what is, not what should be
Machiavelli built his advice on how people actually behave. Plan your business around real incentives and real habits, not the ones in the policy document.
Mercenaries failed Florence. Depend as little as possible on capabilities you cannot control, whether a single agency, platform or supplier.
Bad news and painful changes do less damage delivered together and early. Good news and rewards work better spread out over time.
Firmness is safer than trying to be liked by everyone, but hatred is fatal. Never touch what people feel is rightfully theirs, such as pay, credit or dignity.
Leadership needs both the cunning to see traps and the strength to deter threats. Know which one a situation calls for.
Fortune floods without warning. Use the calm months to build reserves, controls and fallback plans.
The same style wins in one season and loses in another. Ask regularly whether the approach that worked last year still fits today.
Cesare Borgia trusted that new favours would erase old grudges and lost everything. Do not hand power to someone you have wronged.
recall: Why did Machiavelli write The Prince?

After the Medici returned in 1512 he was sacked, then arrested and tortured in 1513 over a plot he was probably not part of. Released in an amnesty, he wrote The Prince on his farm hoping to win the Medici's favour and a job. It did not work.
Is it better to be loved or feared?

Machiavelli said both are best, but if you must choose, fear is safer because love is easily broken while fear of punishment is not. He insisted that a ruler must never become hated, chiefly by leaving people's property and families alone.
What lesson did Machiavelli take from Cesare Borgia?

Cesare showed how a new ruler could build a state through decisive and sometimes brutal action, such as the execution of Remirro de Orco. But he fell after his father's death, partly by trusting an old enemy who became Pope Julius the Second.

Virtù is ability, boldness and capacity to act, while fortuna is chance. Machiavelli thought fortune controlled about half of affairs and compared it to a flooding river that can be managed with embankments built in calm times.
What is meant by armed and unarmed prophets?

Machiavelli observed that Savonarola, who had only persuasion, was destroyed once the people stopped believing him. Leaders who have means to sustain their authority succeed, while those relying on belief alone eventually fall.
note: Machiavelli's life is well documented through his official dispatches and letters, especially the letter to Vettori of 10 December 1513. The torture is documented; the six drops come from his own sonnet to Giuliano de' Medici. The killings of Remirro de Orco and the captains at Senigallia are recorded in his dispatches. Whether The Prince is sincere advice or satire remains debated, though most modern scholars read it as sincere.

One December morning the people of Cesena woke to find Remirro's body lying in two pieces in the town square, a block of wood and a bloody knife beside it. Cesare had taken the order and handed the hatred to someone else. Machiavelli, who was at Cesare's court as Florence's envoy, wrote that the spectacle left the people at once satisfied and stunned.

In 1512 the Medici returned to Florence and Machiavelli lost his job. Months later a plot against them was uncovered, and his name was on a conspirator's list. There is no evidence he was involved. He was arrested and given the strappado: hands tied behind his back, hoisted on a rope, and dropped. He wrote a rueful sonnet from his cell mentioning six drops on his shoulders, and confessed nothing. Then a Medici was elected Pope Leo the Tenth, Florence declared an amnesty, and Machiavelli walked out, jobless and forty-three, to write The Prince.

In December 1513, exiled to his little farm outside Florence, Machiavelli wrote to his friend Vettori describing his days. He snared thrushes, argued with woodcutters and shouted over cards at the inn with the butcher and the miller. But every evening he came home, took off his muddy clothes at the door, and put on the robes of a court official. Dressed properly, he entered the courts of the ancients, asked great men why they acted as they did, and they answered him. For four hours he felt no boredom and feared neither poverty nor death. Those conversations became The Prince.
biz: Machiavelli watched Florence's hired soldiers fail at Pisa and concluded that a ruler who depends on other people's arms stands on borrowed ground. A brokerage living entirely on paid clicks is in the same position: one platform policy change or price rise and the leads stop. Your own arms are SEO content, your own enquiry forms and a reputation that brings repeat and referred customers. This week, measure what share of HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan enquiries came from owned channels last month, set a target to grow it each quarter, and review it alongside cost per lead.
Build dykes while the sun shines

Fortune, Machiavelli said, is a river you cannot stop once it floods, but you can build embankments in calm weather. For Ruby Holdings the floods are predictable in kind if not in timing: an FCA review of financial promotions, a lender leaving the panel, a key staff member off sick. Spend one hour this week writing a one-page risk register: each risk, its early warning sign and the embankment already in place. Check that every advert has a recorded compliance sign-off, and that a second person can run each critical process.
connects: Thucydides' Melian dialogue, where the strong do what they can, is the ancestor of Machiavelli's effective truth about how power really behaves.
Epictetus split life into what is up to us and what is not, much as Machiavelli divided our affairs between virtù and fortune.
Taleb's call to prepare for shocks rather than predict them echoes Machiavelli's dykes built before the river floods.
recap:
Niccolò Machiavelli was born in Florence in fourteen sixty nine, into an old family with little money. His father, a lawyer who loved books, earned a copy of Livy's history of Rome by compiling its index, and the boy grew up on stories of a republic that rose by its own strength. At nine he saw the Medici family's enemies hanged from the government palace windows after a murder in the cathedral. Politics, he learned early, could kill.

In his twenties he watched the friar Savonarola hold Florence spellbound with sermons, then lose the crowd and burn in the main square. The first big idea came from that: armed prophets conquer, unarmed ones are ruined. Persuasion fades, and a leader needs something solid when belief wears thin.

At twenty nine he became a senior official of the republic and spent fourteen years on missions to kings, emperors and popes. He saw hired mercenaries fail at Pisa, so he raised a citizen militia. The second idea: a state that relies on other people's arms stands on borrowed ground.

He studied Cesare Borgia up close, a ruler who let a lieutenant restore order brutally, then had him cut in two in a town square so the hatred died with him. Cesare did almost everything right and still fell when his father the Pope died. The third idea runs through the book. Machiavelli wanted the effective truth of how people behave, not imagined ideal states. It is safer to be feared than loved, he wrote, but never hated, and the surest way to be hated is to take people's property. People judge by what they see, so reputation is a resource.

Then fortune turned. In fifteen twelve the Medici returned, he lost his job, and the following year he was tortured on the rope over a plot he had no part in. Released in an amnesty, he retreated to a small farm. By day he trapped birds and argued over cards. By night he put on court robes and talked with the ancients, and from those conversations came The Prince.

The fourth idea is the river. Fortune, he said, governs about half our affairs, like a flood no one can stop. But in calm weather we can build embankments, and ruin comes to those who built nothing while the sun shone.

The Medici never really took him back. He died in fifteen twenty seven, and The Prince, printed after his death, made his name a byword for wickedness. Most scholars now read it as sincere advice for a broken, invaded Italy.

The line to remember: build your dykes before the flood.
